title: If
author: Rudyard Kipling
summary: A father advises his son on how to become a mature, balanced man. Each 'if' names a quality:

Stanza 1 — keep calm when everyone around loses their head and blames you; trust yourself when all doubt you, yet allow for their doubts; wait without tiring; being lied about, don't lie; being hated, don't hate; yet don't look too good or talk too wise.

Stanza 2 — dream, but don't make dreams your master; think, but don't make thoughts your aim; meet Triumph and Disaster and treat 'those two impostors' just the same; bear to hear your truth twisted by knaves to trap fools, or see your life's work broken and rebuild it with worn-out tools.

Stanza 3 — risk all your winnings on one turn of pitch-and-toss, lose, start again and never complain; force heart, nerve and sinew to serve you long after they are spent, holding on when nothing is left but the Will that says 'Hold on!'

Stanza 4 — talk with crowds and keep your virtue, walk with kings and not lose the common touch; let neither foes nor loving friends hurt you; let all men count with you, but none too much; fill 'the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds' worth of distance run' — then 'Yours is the Earth and everything that's in it, and — which is more — you'll be a Man, my son!'

Rudyard Kipling won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1907. 'If—' was first published in 'Brother Square-Toes' in Rewards and Fairies (1910), as a tribute to Leander Starr Jameson. His autobiography is Something of Myself (1937).
Form: a didactic poem in four stanzas of eight lines (octaves); alternating rhyme (ABAB …). It is close to a dramatic monologue — one speaker advising a silent listener.
Devices: anaphora (repeated 'If you can'), personification and metaphor (Triumph and Disaster as 'impostors'), alliteration ('treat those two'), assonance, irony ('wait and not be tired by waiting').
Reported speech of questions: asked/enquired/wondered + if/whether (yes-no questions) or the wh-word; statement word order; tense and pronoun changes.
mcq: Why does Kipling describe 'Triumph' and 'Disaster' as 'impostors'?
They are permanent states of life
They deceive us into losing perspective
'Keep your head when all about you are losing theirs' means —
How does the poem advise handling waiting, lies and hatred?
Wait impatiently and respond with lies
Be patient but repay hatred with hatred
Wait patiently, avoid lying and don't give in to hatred
starting again with whatever strength is left after a failure
finding a middle way in a conflict
The repetition of 'If you can' at the beginning of lines is an example of —
What best describes 'the Will' in the poem?
The spirit of never giving up against odds

sa2: Neither lasts and neither shows the true value of a person. Success can make us proud and failure can crush us, so both deceive us; we should treat them alike.
What does the poet mean by keeping or losing one's head?
Keeping one's head means staying calm and clear-minded in a crisis; losing it means panicking and acting without thought.
Why should we not 'look too good, nor talk too wise'?
Because we should stay humble and natural. Pretending to be better or wiser than we are seems arrogant and self-righteous.
What should we do in the face of failure, according to the poet?
We should start again from the beginning with whatever strength we have, without complaining, and rebuild what has been broken even with worn-out tools.
What does 'not make dreams your master' mean?
We should dream and plan, but not let dreams rule us or lose touch with reality; we must also act practically.
How can friends harm us? Why should 'none count too much'?
Loving friends can hurt us through our attachment and by misleading or disappointing us. If we depend too much on anyone we lose independence, so we should value all but rely on none too much.
What is meant by 'fill the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds' worth of distance run'?
Time never forgives waste; we should use every moment fully and purposefully, doing as much as we can in the time we have.
sa3: What qualities does Kipling expect his son to have? List any four with reasons.

Calmness in crisis, so others' panic does not affect him; self-trust balanced with respect for others' doubts; patience and honesty — not lying or hating in return; and perseverance — starting again after losses and holding on by sheer will. These make him a mature 'Man'.
How does the poem emphasise perseverance and determination?

It asks us to rebuild our broken life's work with worn-out tools, to start again after losing all our winnings without complaint, and to force heart, nerve and sinew to serve us long after they are spent, holding on by the Will alone.

or: What is the ultimate reward mentioned in the poem?
If the son can fulfil all these 'ifs', the whole Earth and everything in it will be his — and, more important, he will become a true Man: mature, balanced and morally strong.

sa3: Why is 'If' called a didactic poem?

A didactic poem teaches a lesson. Here a father instructs his son on how to live — staying calm, honest, humble, patient and determined — so that he becomes a mature man. The whole poem is a list of moral lessons.
